introduction: The Visual Arts School-Based Assessment is a body of practical work supported by a process journal, developed through research and reflection and presented for assessment and exhibition. Marks are given for the range and quality of the practical work, the evidence of research and development, the technical competence and use of media, the coherence of the body of work and the quality of the journal and evaluation. Check the current CSEC syllabus and your teacher's guidance for the required number of pieces, areas of study, sizes and mark allocation.

tasks.title: Research and stimulus
tasks.explanation: Record the theme or stimulus for your body of work, the visual and written research carried out, the artists and traditions studied, and how these informed your ideas, with dated sketches, photographs and sources.

tasks.title: Development of ideas
tasks.explanation: Show the development of each piece from thumbnail sketches and compositional studies through trials of media and colour to the final design, including the problems found and the changes made.

tasks.title: Practical work
tasks.explanation: Produce the required number and range of pieces in a variety of media and areas, each resolved, well-crafted and consistent with your theme.

tasks.title: Journal and documentation
tasks.explanation: Keep a complete, dated process journal covering research, decisions, technical notes, evaluations and documentation of finished pieces, correctly citing all sources.

tasks.title: Presentation and evaluation
tasks.explanation: Present the work mounted or framed and labelled, with a written statement evaluating the body of work, your technical progress and what you would do differently.

sampleTitle: A body of work on market women: five pieces in charcoal, acrylic, lino print and mixed media

sample.body: The theme began with a photograph of my aunt's stall and three afternoons of observational drawing in the market, where I produced six gesture drawings of vendors and shoppers and two tonal charcoal studies of produce arranged in basins. I then compared the work of Albert Huie for the way he groups figures in shallow space and used his market paintings as a reference for composition, noted in the journal with the source. Twelve thumbnails explored arrangements of two and three figures before I chose an asymmetrical grouping with the largest figure at the left third and a diagonal of basins leading to the right. Media trials followed: a lino test plate was cut to check the bold shapes of hands and produce, acrylic colour tests established an earth palette of burnt sienna, yellow ochre, black and white with one warm accent, and a mixed-media study combined acrylic with torn newspaper and fabric from the market itself. Each trial is dated in the journal with the result recorded.
sample.tips: Show the trial, the reason and the outcome. A journal with rejected options scores better than one showing only the finished piece.

sample.body: The five pieces are mounted in matching off-white acid-free window mounts with a 4 cm border and labelled on the reverse with title, date, media, dimensions and my name, and photographs of each piece at full resolution are filed with the digital portfolio. The pieces are sequenced so that the tonal drawings lead into the lino print and the mixed media work closes the theme. My evaluation finds that the strongest piece is the charcoal grouping, where the figure structure held from the drawing stage, and the weakest is the second acrylic painting, in which I crowded the background with detail that competes with the focal point - the same fault I had already identified in an earlier lino print and failed to correct. My plan for the next body of work is to make compositional thumbnails mandatory before painting and to work at a larger scale so that the figures have space.
sample.tips: Evaluate specific pieces and specific decisions, and name the change you will make next time.

marking: Marks reward thorough and cited research, clearly developed ideas, competent and varied practical work of high craft, a complete and honest process journal, professional presentation and a thoughtful evaluation of the body of work.

categories.comment: The theme is stated and traced to its source: my own photograph of my aunt's stall, three afternoons of observational drawing in the market, six gesture drawings and two tonal studies of produce in basins, with Albert Huie's market paintings studied in reproduction and every source cited by artist, title and where it was seen.

Twelve thumbnails are listed with the arrangement each one tried and why eleven were rejected, the chosen asymmetrical grouping is drawn out with its tonal plan counted, and the three media trials are recorded with the reason for each and the outcome, including the lino shapes that closed up and had to be re-cut.

Five resolved pieces are documented with medium, size, aspect ratio, date and studio hours, covering drawing, printmaking, painting and mixed media, and the two pieces the guide's own sample block singles out are named honestly: the charcoal grouping is the strongest and the acrylic-based work with the crowded background is the weakest.

The journal runs from week 1 to week 10 with the dates of every entry, the number of entries in each week, four problems recorded with the change made or the reason no change was made in time, and the technical notes, colour decisions and photographs of each finished piece filed with the citations.

The five pieces are mounted in matching off-white acid-free window mounts with a 4 cm border, labelled on the reverse with title, date, media, dimensions and my name, hung in the sequence the guide describes inside the exhibition bay with the run measured, and closed by the artist's statement and the evaluation of every piece.

pages.heading: Cover page and contents of this Visual Arts SBA
pages.body: BODY OF WORK: A body of work on market women: five pieces in charcoal, acrylic, lino print and mixed media. This is the written record of the portfolio: the research, the development, the five pieces with their measurements, the process journal and the presentation, laid out in the order of the five parts the guide sets out in Table 1. No picture is reproduced here. Each finished piece is described in words, with its medium, its size in centimetres, its aspect ratio, the date it was completed and the studio hours it took, so the work can be read and checked on screen; in the real submission each of those pieces would also be photographed and the photograph filed with the journal and the digital portfolio.

pages.heading: Research: the market-women stimulus, the artists studied and the sources
pages.body:
The stimulus is the market I walk through on the way to school. In week 1 I photographed my aunt's stall: the basins of produce stacked in a diagonal, the hands of the two women who sell there, and the shallow space between the stalls and the wall. Three afternoons of observational drawing in the market followed, in which I made six gesture drawings of vendors and shoppers to catch the way the figures stand, and two tonal charcoal studies of the produce arranged in the basins to work out how much dark the picture could carry before it stopped reading. The theme became the women who hold the stall rather than the produce: five pieces that keep the same shallow space and the same diagonal of basins.

The written research is small and specific. I studied Albert Huie's market paintings in reproduction for the way he groups figures in shallow space, with the heads close to the top of the picture and the crowd closing in behind, and for the way a diagonal of baskets or basins carries the eye across the picture without a drawn line. What I took from him is a compositional habit, not an image: no reproduction is copied, traced or reproduced in this body of work. I then read the part of our syllabus that describes the body of work and its five assessment parts, and wrote out what each part asks for before I began, which is why each piece below is documented rather than only described.
bullets: Own material: one photograph of the stall, six gesture drawings, two tonal charcoal studies, all dated in the journal.
Artist reference: two Albert Huie market paintings studied in reproduction, used for shallow-space grouping and for the diagonal, nothing copied.
Syllabus: the five assessment parts and the areas to be covered, written into the journal in week 1.
Permission: the two traders allowed me to draw and photograph at their stalls, and one gave me the market fabric used in the mixed-media piece.
Nothing is cited that I did not see or make, and no source is listed without saying what it gave me.

pages.heading: Method: how the research, the studies and the five pieces were made and recorded
pages.body:
The work ran for ten weeks and every week is dated in the journal, so anything in this record can be traced to the week it happened. The order was fixed at the start and followed: research first, then development, then the pieces one at a time, with the journal written on the day rather than at the end. Week 1 was the photograph and the first afternoon in the market; weeks 2 and 3 were the drawing and the tonal studies; weeks 4 to 5 were the thumbnails and the choice of composition; weeks 6 to 10 were the five finished pieces, one a week, with the mounting and the presentation done in the last of them and the media trials fitted in before the piece that needed them.

Every finished piece is recorded the same way, so that the five rows of Table 6 can be compared: the title, the area and the medium, the width and the height in centimetres measured on the dry piece with a steel rule, the aspect ratio worked out from those two measurements, the size after mounting, the week it was finished and the studio hours spent on it. The studio hours are counted from the journal, which notes the time at the start and the end of each session, and they come to 69 hours across the five pieces. The mounts add 0.38 square metres of board to the 0.96 square metres of paper, canvas board and board the pieces themselves cover, because each mount carries a 4 cm border on all four sides and Table 6 shows both measurements for every piece.

The recording rules were kept without exception. The journal is dated; each entry says what was done, what went wrong and what was decided; rejected options are kept rather than thrown away, which is why eleven thumbnails and four problems are still in the record. Photographs of every finished piece were taken in daylight on the same day the piece was finished, at full resolution, and filed with the digital portfolio and backed up on two devices. Nothing in this record was written from memory at the end of the ten weeks.

pages.heading: Development: the dated journal log, week by week
pages.body:
This is the spine of the process journal: 46 dated entries over ten weeks, never fewer than three in a week and never a week without work recorded. Each entry carries the day, what was done, what was decided and, where something went wrong, what was done about it. The entries that matter most are the ones about the problems, because those are the ones that changed the work: the toned paper was too grey in week 7 and white chalk was added to the highlights; the lino plate was over-cut in week 8 and a section had to be re-cut and printed again; the acrylic ground dried too fast in the heat in week 9 and the board was wetted and painted in sections.

The journal is also where the sources are cited. The Albert Huie reference sits in week 3, beside the drawing where the shallow-space grouping was first tried, rather than in a list at the end, so the reader can see which decision it affected. The photographs of the finished pieces are filed against the week the piece was completed, and the digital folder is dated the same way.

pages.heading: Development: the twelve thumbnails, the tonal plan and the three media trials
pages.body:
Twelve thumbnails were drawn before any piece was started, on one sheet, each about the size of a playing card. Eleven were rejected and the reasons are written on the sheet in my own hand: six for crowding at the back of the stall, three for no clear focal point and two for figures too equal in scale. The chosen arrangement is asymmetrical: the largest figure stands at the left third, a diagonal of basins leads to the right, and the space in front is kept empty so the eye has somewhere to rest.

The tonal plan of that composition was fixed before the piece was begun and then counted rather than guessed. The three masses were marked in the chosen thumbnail - dark, middle and light - and after piece 2, the charcoal grouping, was finished a ten-by-ten grid was laid over its photograph and every square was marked the same way. That count is the one recorded here, and it gives 34 squares of dark, 41 of middle and 25 of light, which is the whole hundred. The dark is carried by two charcoal masses, the figure and the shadowed basins; the middle is the toned paper itself; the light is a small number of chalk highlights kept for the shoulders and the produce. Keeping the lights to about a quarter of the picture is the rule I set myself after the first tonal study went grey all over.

Three media trials were then recorded, each with the reason it was made and the result: lino test plate, acrylic colour tests and mixed-media study.

pages.heading: Results: the five finished pieces, with medium, size, mount and date
pages.body:
Five pieces were finished, and no sixth was left half done at the end of the ten weeks. In the order they are hung, the sequence opens with the two drawings, moves to the lino print and closes with the mixed-media piece, which is the order the guide's own sample block describes: the tonal drawings lead into the lino print and the mixed media work closes the theme. Each piece is measured dry, in centimetres, width then height, and each measurement is given twice in Table 6, once for the work itself and once for the work in its mount, which is 4 cm larger on every side.

Read across the five rows and the body of work covers four areas - drawing, printmaking, painting and mixed media - and four media - charcoal, lino, acrylic and a mixed-media combination of acrylic with torn newspaper and market fabric. The pieces themselves cover 0.96 square metres of paper, toned paper, cartridge, canvas board and board, and in their mounts they cover 1.35 square metres, so the mounts add 0.38 square metres of paper and board to the body of work. The studio hours in the last column are counted from the journal and come to 69 hours, of which 34 were spent on the two acrylic-based pieces.

Two of the five rows have to be named honestly here rather than in the evaluation. Piece 2, the charcoal grouping, is the strongest of the five: the figure structure that was worked out in the gesture drawings held all the way through, and the tonal plan was kept. Piece 5, the mixed-media piece, is the weakest: its background is crowded with detail that competes with the focal point, which is the same fault recorded against the lino print in week 8 and not corrected in time.
bullets: Five pieces, four media, four areas of study, none left unfinished.
Every piece signed and dated, dry before it was mounted, photographed in daylight before it was mounted.
Sizes measured with a steel rule; mounts calculated as measurement plus 8 cm on each axis.
Strongest: piece 2, the charcoal grouping. Weakest: piece 5, the mixed-media piece, whose background is crowded.

pages.heading: Results: the process journal checked point by point against the checklist
pages.body:
The guide leaves a checklist of sixteen items, and this page answers it item by item rather than asserting that it was met. All sixteen are answered: the table gives the item, and the page and the evidence behind it. Two of the sixteen are worth reading twice. Item 11 asks for the problems and the solutions, and four problems are recorded, three of them solved and one of them not solved in time - the crowded background of the mixed-media piece, which is named as a weakness on page 6 and again in the evaluation rather than quietly dropped. Item 13 asks for the work to be backed up, and the digital folder holds the full-size photographs of all five pieces, the twelve thumbnails and the three trials, copied to two drives.

The journal is the piece of paper a teacher can check against the work itself: the entry for a week names the piece, the medium, what was decided and what the result looked like, and the entry for the week a piece was finished carries the photograph. That is why the journal is treated here as evidence and not as a diary, and why the rejected options were kept.

pages.heading: Presentation: the mounts, the labels, the exhibition hang and the artist's statement
pages.body:
The five pieces are presented as one body of work, not as five separate pictures. Each is mounted in a matching off-white acid-free window mount with a 4 cm border on all four sides, so the mount adds 8 cm on each axis and the five mounted pieces measure 50 x 38 cm, 68 x 53 cm, 38 x 48 cm, 58 x 48 cm, 63 x 53 cm. On the reverse of each mount is a label carrying the title, the date, the medium, the dimensions and my name, written out in full in the format "Two Vendors, Shallow Space, charcoal, 60 x 45 cm". The work is hung in the order of Table 6, left to right, with the same 6 cm gap between the mounts, so the run along the wall is 50 + 68 + 38 + 58 + 63 cm of mount plus 24 cm of gaps, which is 301 cm. The exhibition bay is 360 cm wide, so the body of work fits with 59 cm to spare, and that spare space is used for the artist's statement rather than for another piece. The centre line of every piece is set at 150 cm from the floor.

ARTIST'S STATEMENT, mounted beside the work. "These five pieces are about the two women who hold the stall I walk past on the way to school: their hands, the basin of produce they arrange and re-arrange all morning, and the shallow space between the stall and the wall behind it. I worked in charcoal first to learn how much dark the picture could carry, then cut a lino plate to see the same shapes reduced to their boldest, then painted, and finished with the mixed-media piece, which is where the market's own material - torn newspaper and a piece of fabric given to me by one of the traders - comes into the work. What I want the five pieces to say together is that the stall is held by people and not by the produce." The statement is printed at the size of the labels and hung at the same height, so a visitor reads it before turning to the pieces.

pages.heading: Discussion: what worked, what did not, and why
pages.body:
The part of the work that held from the start was the drawing. The six gesture drawings were made quickly and without correction, and the figure structure they settled - a large standing figure with the weight on one hip, a second figure turned into the space - survived into both charcoal pieces and into the mixed media piece. That is why piece 2 is the strongest: the tonal plan, 34 squares of dark, 41 of middle and 25 of light on the ten-by-ten grid, was decided before the charcoal went down and was kept.

Three things did not work. The lino plate was over-cut in the top left corner in week 8; the shapes of the hands had closed up in the test plate too, which should have warned me, and the section had to be re-cut and the edition reprinted. The acrylic ground dried too fast in the heat in week 9, which pulled the paint into streaks; wetting the board and working in sections fixed it, but the fix cost most of a session. And the toned paper for piece 2 was greyer than the sample I bought, so the first blocking-in was too flat and the highlights had to be added in chalk afterwards, which is why the lights in the finished piece are chalk and not paper.

The failure that matters is piece 5. The background of the mixed-media piece is crowded with detail - torn newspaper behind the figures, a second row of stalls, lettering left showing - and that detail competes with the focal point instead of sitting behind it. The same fault is in the journal against the lino print in week 8, where the shapes behind the hands were cut too busy, so it is a fault I had already diagnosed and did not correct when I met it the second time. The reason is plain: the mixed-media piece was made in the last two weeks and I had already spent 51 of the 69 studio hours, so when the background began to fill up I did not stop to take it back. Two things would have prevented it: keeping the tonal plan beside the piece for the mixed-media work as I had for the charcoal, and leaving the background in three flat shapes instead of introducing lettering that had to be covered over later.

The choices that worked are worth naming too, because they are the ones I will carry forward. Measuring every piece before mounting it kept the sizes comparable, so the five mounts read as one body of work: the run across the wall is 301 cm and every piece sits on the same centre line. Keeping the rejected thumbnails turned a choice into an argument on paper, and the tonal count made the darkest decision in the charcoal measurable rather than a matter of taste.
bullets: Held: the gesture-drawing structure, the chosen composition, the tonal plan and the measured mounts.
Failed: the over-cut lino plate, the fast-drying acrylic ground, the too-grey toned paper, and the crowded background of piece 5.
Diagnosed twice, corrected once: the crowding in the lino print and then in the mixed-media piece.
Carry forward: the tonal plan beside the piece, three flat background shapes, and thumbnails before any painting.

pages.heading: Conclusion: my evaluation of each piece and of the body of work as a whole
pages.body:
Piece 1, the tonal study of basins, does its job as the first piece: it established how much dark the paper would take and it taught me that the light had to be kept small. Piece 2, the charcoal grouping, is the strongest of the five. The figure structure held, the shallow space reads, and the diagonal of basins carries the eye without being drawn in as an arrow. Piece 3, the lino print, is the most economical: the reduction to bold shapes sharpened my understanding of the figures, although the shapes behind the hands were cut too busy, which was the first appearance of the fault that recurs in piece 5. Piece 4, the acrylic painting, is technically the most secure of the painted pieces: the earth palette of burnt sienna, yellow ochre, black and white with the single warm accent holds together and the ground was painted in sections without streaks after the change of method. Piece 5, the mixed-media piece, closes the theme as the guide's sequence asks, and it is the weakest of the five, for the reason given twice in this record: its background is crowded and competes with the figures.

The body of work as a whole is coherent. The shallow space and the diagonal of basins run through all five pieces; four media and four areas are covered across five works; the five sizes were chosen so that the mounts would read as one exhibition rather than five pictures; and the strongest and the weakest piece are both named here rather than averaged away. Where the body of work is weaker is in its range of scale: every piece is between 30 and 60 cm wide, and the figures are consequently all about the same size on the wall.

For the next body of work I will change four things, all of them aimed at the problems recorded here and in Table 8: compositional thumbnails and the tonal plan will be pinned beside the piece while it is being made, not only before; the background of any crowded subject will be reduced to three flat shapes before any detail is added; the largest piece will be at least a metre wide, so that the figures have room and the scale range is real; and the last piece will be started with two weeks still in hand, because both faults that survived into the finished work happened in the final weeks.
bullets: Piece 1: the tonal study that set the dark-light rule. Sound but slight.
Piece 2: the charcoal grouping, the strongest of the five, and the measurement standard for the others.
Piece 3: the lino print, economical and sharp, with the busy background shapes that recur in piece 5.
Piece 4: the acrylic painting, technically secure, the palette and the ground solved.
Piece 5: the mixed-media piece, formally the weakest because of the crowded background.

pages.heading: Sources, permissions and honesty note for this worked example
pages.body:
SOURCES. Nothing is used in this body of work that I did not make or see. The photograph of the stall is my own, taken in week 1. The drawings, the tonal studies, the thumbnails, the three trials, the lino edition and the painted pieces are all mine. Albert Huie's market paintings were studied in reproduction for compositional habits only - grouping figures in shallow space, and letting a diagonal carry the eye - and no reproduction, in whole or in part, is copied, traced, photographed for the portfolio or reproduced in any of the five pieces or in this record. The syllabus extract used on page 1 is paraphrased in my own words and the five parts are listed by name, not quoted.

PERMISSIONS. The manager of the market gave permission for drawing and photography in the market on three afternoons, and the two traders whose stalls are the subject agreed to be drawn and photographed, on the understanding that no face would be shown in close-up and no name would be used; the figures in the work are seen from behind, in profile or at a distance for that reason. The market fabric used in the mixed-media piece was given to me by one of those traders and its use is recorded in the journal with her agreement. The school's permission note for off-site work is filed with the journal.

HONESTY NOTE ON THIS RECORD. This document is the written record of an invented portfolio, written as a worked example for CSEC Compass so that a student can see what a complete body of work looks like when it is documented. The candidate, the school, the market traders and all five pieces are invented, and every figure in this record - the sizes, the mounted sizes, the aspect ratios, the studio hours, the tonal count, the journal entries and the hang measurements - belongs to that invented work. No artwork is reproduced here: the pieces are described and measured in words, because a photograph of an invented piece would not be a photograph of anything. What is real in this document is the method: how the research is cited, how the measurements are taken and recorded, how the rejected options and the problems are kept, and how the checklist is answered point by point.
